newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to stick by his budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to stick by his budget.

text.p: President Clinton will stick by the budget he submitted to Congress last month, rejecting calls from Republicans to completely revamp it, White House budget director Franklin Raines said Sunday.
"We are ready to work from the president's budget," Raines said on NBC's "Meet the Press" programme.
He said that the White House hopes that it can strike a budget deal with Congress by April, despite complaints from Republicans that Clinton's proposed plan does not balance the budget by 2002.
"We think that there is no reason we can't," Raines said.

Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Dominici, a New Mexico Republican, said that he would offer a Republican alternative budget if Clinton did not make deeper cuts in entitlement programmes such as Medicare to balance the budget.
"We can produce a budget," he said on CNN's "Late Edition" programme. "In fact, I will recommend one if we can't get an agreement on entitlements."

He said under his proposal, "there will be no new programs" and discretionary spending would be limited. He said he would cut at least three times the $51 billion proposed reduction that Clinton would make in entitlements.

Clinton sent Congress a $1.69 trillion budget proposal that cut $98.4 billion in taxes over five years, slashed $100 billion from Medicare health care for the elderly and reached a $17 billion surplus in 2002.
Republican budget leaders said if the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office economic assumptions were applied, the budget would post a large deficit in 2002.
In the last Congress, budget negotiations fell apart and forced two government shutdowns that the public blamed on Republicans.
